For a discussion of possible carcino- genic effects in children given vitamin K intramuscularly, see Carcinogenicity, p.1996. Effects on mortality. Although vitamin supplements have been widely taken in the hope of improving mortality from vari- ous diseases, a large systematic review1 concluded that there was no evidence that antoxidant vitamin supplements improved mor- tality, and some, such as vitamin A, betacarotene, and vitamin E, might increase it. For mention of possible adverse effects on mortality with beta- carotene supplementation, see Effects on Mortality, p.1931. For discussion on the effects on mortality with Vitamin A, see p.1972. For mention of possible beneficial effects of high serum ascorbic acid levels on all-cause mortality, see under Vitamin C, p.1984. For mention of possible dose-dependent adverse effects on mortality with use of vitamin E, see Effects on Mortality, p.1993. For discussion of the effects of various antoxidant vita- mins on cardiovascular disease and cancer, see Prophylaxis of Ischaemic Heart Disease, below, and Prophylaxis of Malignant Neoplasms, p.1927, below. 1. Bjelakovic G, et al. Antioxidant supplements for prevention of mortality in healthy participants and patients with various dis- eases. Available in The Cochrane Database of Systematic Re- views; Issue 2. Chichester: John Wiley; 2008 (accessed 18/06/08). Human requirements. Vitamins and trace elements are es- sential nutrients and in many countries guidance has been pub- lished concerning their intake. In the UK various terms are used to define intake:1 • estimated average requirement (EAR) is used for the require- ments of energy, proteins, vitamins, or minerals of a group of people and usually about half will need more and half less than the specified figure • lower reference nutrient intake (LRNI) is applied to proteins, vitamins, or minerals and is that amount that is enough for only a few people who have low needs • reference nutrient intake (RNI) is also applied to proteins, vi- tamins, or minerals and is an amount that is enough, or more than enough, for about 97% of people in a group • a safe intake is used to indicate an intake or range of intakes where there is not enough information to estimate EAR, LR- NI, or RNI, but rather it is an amount enough for almost eve- ryone but is not so large as to cause undesirable effects • dietary reference value (DRV) is used to cover EAR, LRNI, RNI, and safe intake.
